1: Benjamin Franklin (1706–1790) was an American printer, scientist, and statesman — one of the Founding Fathers and the self-made man of the new republic. His unfinished Autobiography, written in stages from 1771, recounts his rise from a runaway Boston apprentice; the section here lays out his celebrated scheme of thirteen virtues for moral self-improvement.
2: John Milton (1608–1674) was an English poet and political writer, later author of the epic Paradise Lost. These are among his earliest verses — written in his school and college years and including the ode On the Morning of Christ’s Nativity — which open his collected English poems.
3: Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 B.C.) was a Roman statesman and orator whose prose became a model of classical Latin. On Friendship (Lælius de Amicitia) is a short dialogue in which the aged Roman Lælius, lately bereaved of a dear friend, reflects with two younger companions on what friendship is.
4: Jacob Grimm (1785–1863), with his brother Wilhelm, collected the German folk tales that became the famous Grimms’ Fairy Tales. This story tells of a poor fisherman who catches a magical flounder, and of a wife who keeps sending him back to ask the fish for more.
5: Giuseppe Mazzini (1805–1872) was an Italian revolutionary and writer, a driving force of the Risorgimento that unified Italy. Byron and Goethe is a critical essay in which he sets the two great poets of the age side by side and asks what each of them represents.
6: Virgil (70–19 B.C.) was Rome’s greatest poet, author of the national epic the Æneid, which follows the Trojan hero Æneas from the ruins of Troy toward the founding of Rome. In these pages the ghost of Hector warns Æneas on the night the city falls, and he gathers his family to flee.
7: The Thousand and One Nights (the Arabian Nights) is a great medieval collection of Middle Eastern and South Asian tales, gathered over many centuries. Its frame story opens here: a betrayed king who weds and executes a new bride each dawn, until the clever Scheherazade begins to tell him a tale.
8: The Book of Job, one of the poetic books of the Hebrew Bible, is an ancient meditation on suffering and faith. It opens with Job, a prosperous and upright man, as a wager in heaven sets in motion the calamities that befall him.
9: Sir Francis Drake (c. 1540–1596) was an English sea captain and privateer, the first Englishman to sail around the world and a scourge of Spanish shipping. Sir Francis Drake Revived, compiled by Philip Nichols from the seamen’s own notes, narrates his daring 1572 raid on the Spanish treasure-port of Nombre de Dios with just fifty-two men.
10: Euripides (c. 480–406 B.C.) was the last of the three great tragedians of classical Athens. The Bacchæ dramatizes the arrival of the god Dionysus in Thebes, where King Pentheus sets himself against the god and against the women swept up in his ecstatic rites.
11: Alexander Hamilton (1757–1804) was a Founding Father and the first U.S. Secretary of the Treasury, who built the financial system of the young nation. The Federalist is the series of essays he wrote with James Madison and John Jay, urging the states to ratify the newly drafted Constitution.
12: Edmund Burke (1729–1797) was an Irish-born British statesman and philosopher, best known for his Reflections on the Revolution in France and his writings on the sublime and beautiful. On Taste is the introductory essay he prefaced to that treatise, an inquiry into whether our judgments of beauty and art rest on any standard shared by all people.
13: Jean-Jacques Rousseau (1712–1778) was a Geneva-born philosopher of the French Enlightenment whose ideas on natural freedom and the social contract helped inspire the French Revolution. His Discourse on the Origin of Inequality (1755) traces humankind back to an imagined “state of nature” to ask where the divisions among men first arose.
14: The Fundamental Orders of Connecticut were adopted in 1639 by the settlers of the river towns of Hartford, Windsor, and Wethersfield. This brief founding document sets out the frame of government for the young colony — its officers, its elections, and its assemblies.
15: Omar Khayyám (1048–1131) was a Persian mathematician, astronomer, and poet. The Rubáiyát is a collection of his quatrains, made famous in English by Edward FitzGerald’s 1859 translation — brief, self-contained verses on life, time, and fate.
16: Aesop was a storyteller of ancient Greece (traditionally the 6th century B.C.) whose name attaches to a famous body of Fables — short animal tales, each carrying a moral. This selection gathers a number of them, among them the brief tale of the old woman and the empty wine jar.
17: Benjamin Franklin (1706–1790) — printer, scientist, and Founding Father — addressed his Autobiography to his son. These opening pages look back to his English ancestors and the Boston household he was born into, the youngest son of a candle-and-soap maker.
18: Aristophanes (c. 446–386 B.C.) was the great comic playwright of ancient Athens. The Frogs sends the god Dionysus and his slave down to the underworld — its croaking frog-chorus gives the play its name — on a quest to bring a great tragic poet back to the living.
19: Edgar Allan Poe (1809–1849) was an American poet and storyteller, a master of the macabre and a pioneer of the detective tale. The Poetic Principle is a lecture-essay in which he examines what poetry is and how it works, illustrating with poems he admired.
20: John Keats (1795–1821) was an English Romantic poet, celebrated for the rich music of his verse. The Eve of St. Agnes is a narrative poem set on a bitter medieval night when, by old superstition, a maiden may dream of her lover — and young Porphyro steals into the castle of his beloved Madeline.
21: Hans Christian Andersen (1805–1875) was a Danish author whose original fairy tales are read the world over. The Nightingale tells of a Chinese emperor who comes to prize a plain little bird for its song — until a jewelled mechanical nightingale arrives at his court.
22: Pierre Corneille (1606–1684) was a founding master of French classical tragedy. Polyeucte is his drama set in Roman Armenia, where a newly converted Christian nobleman must weigh his faith against his marriage, his friends, and the power of the state.
23: Blaise Pascal (1623–1662) was a French mathematician, physicist, and religious thinker. The Art of Persuasion is a short essay in which he considers how people actually come to believe what they believe, and how one mind may rightly move another.
24: Homer is the traditional author of the ancient Greek epics; the Odyssey recounts the long voyage home of Odysseus after the Trojan War. In this episode his ship must pass the Sirens, whose song lures sailors to their death.
25: Robert Burns (1759–1796) is Scotland’s national poet, who wrote in the vivid Scots tongue of country life. This selection gathers some of his best-loved poems — among them To a Mouse, addressed to a field-mouse turned out of its nest by his plough, and the comic tale Tam o’ Shanter.
26: Herodotus (c. 484–425 B.C.), the Greek “Father of History,” travelled the ancient world gathering its stories. An Account of Egypt is the part of his Histories given over to that land — its river and customs, its kings, priests, and wonders, as he heard them told.
27: Dante Alighieri (1265–1321) was the Florentine poet of the Divine Comedy, the great medieval vision of a journey through Hell, Purgatory, and Paradise. In these canti the poet, near the summit of the mountain of Purgatory, comes at last to his long-awaited meeting with Beatrice.
28: Thomas à Kempis (c. 1380–1471) was a German-Dutch monk and writer. The Imitation of Christ is his classic of Christian devotion; these short chapters meditate on the inner life — on simplicity, humility, and purity of heart.
29: Charles Darwin (1809–1882) was the English naturalist whose later work transformed biology. The Voyage of the Beagle is the journal of his five-year survey expedition; here he reaches Tierra del Fuego, at the storm-battered southern tip of South America, and describes its land and its people.
30: Sophocles (c. 496–406 B.C.) was one of the three great tragedians of ancient Athens. Antigone opens after a civil war at Thebes, where the princess Antigone resolves to bury her dead brother in defiance of the king’s edict, on pain of death.
31: Miguel de Cervantes (1547–1616) was a Spanish soldier and writer whose Don Quixote (1605–1615) is often called the first modern novel. It follows an aging country gentleman who, his head filled with old tales of chivalry, sets out across Spain as a wandering knight in search of adventures.
